text.title: Salt and the Trans-Saharan Trade
text.body:
For most of human history, salt was far more valuable than it is today. Before refrigeration, it was the main way to preserve meat and fish, and people and animals also need it in their diet. In regions without salt deposits or access to the sea, it had to be imported, often over great distances.

One of the best-known examples is the trade that crossed the Sahara Desert for many centuries. In the north of the desert, salt was cut from dry lake beds in large slabs. Camel caravans carried these slabs south to West African trading towns such as Timbuktu, where salt was scarce. There, merchants exchanged it for gold, which was mined further south, as well as for ivory and cloth.

This exchange had effects far beyond the goods themselves. Trading cities grew wealthy by taxing the caravans that passed through them, and rulers who controlled the routes became powerful. Ideas, languages and scholarship also travelled along the same paths, turning some market towns into centres of learning.

options: It was used to make coins for trade.
It was used to keep food from spoiling.
It could be found only in the desert.
It was used to build trading towns.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 1: before refrigeration, salt 'was the main way to preserve meat and fish'.

questions.explanation: Salt had to be carried to towns like Timbuktu because there was little of it there, so 'scarce' means in short supply.

options: Their power depended partly on trade.
They kept scholars out of their cities.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says rulers 'who controlled the routes became powerful', so their power was linked to the caravan trade.

To explain why camels were used in the desert

questions.explanation: Timbuktu is introduced with 'such as' as an example of the trading towns where caravans exchanged salt for other goods.

text.title: Building with Adobe
text.body:
Adobe is one of the oldest building materials in the world. It is made by mixing clay-rich soil with water and a little straw or grass, pressing the mixture into wooden moulds, and leaving the bricks to dry in the sun. Because the ingredients are found almost everywhere and no fuel is needed to bake the bricks, adobe is cheap and easy to produce.

Adobe buildings are especially common in hot, dry regions, such as parts of North Africa, the Middle East and the southwestern United States. Their thick walls absorb heat slowly during the day, so the rooms inside stay cool. At night, the walls release the stored heat, which keeps the inside warm when the desert air turns cold.

Adobe also has weaknesses. Heavy rain can wash away unprotected walls, so builders often cover them with a layer of plaster, and the walls must be repaired regularly. Even so, many adobe buildings have survived for hundreds of years.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1: the ingredients 'are found almost everywhere and no fuel is needed to bake the bricks'.

text.title: The Testing Effect
text.body:
Most students regard tests purely as a means of measuring what they have learned. A substantial body of research in cognitive psychology, however, suggests that the act of retrieving information from memory is itself a powerful way of learning it. This phenomenon, known as the testing effect, has been replicated with materials ranging from vocabulary lists to complex scientific texts.

In a typical experiment, participants study a passage and then either reread it or attempt to recall its content without looking. On a test given a few minutes later, rereaders often perform as well as, or slightly better than, the recall group. After a delay of several days, though, the pattern reverses: those who practised retrieval remember considerably more. Rereading, it seems, produces a sense of familiarity that learners mistake for durable knowledge.

Researchers attribute the benefit partly to effort. Retrieval that is difficult, but ultimately successful, appears to strengthen memory traces more than retrieval that is easy. This helps explain why spacing practice sessions apart, which makes recall harder, tends to enhance long-term retention.

questions.prompt: The word "durable" in paragraph 2 is closest in meaning to
options: detailed
long-lasting
practical
accurate
questions.explanation: Rereaders' knowledge fades after several days, so the knowledge they think they have is not 'durable', that is, long-lasting.

questions.prompt: According to paragraph 2, how do rereaders perform on a test given a few minutes after studying?
options: Much worse than participants who recalled the text
Worse than they themselves had expected to perform
About as well as, or a little better than, the recall group
Better on scientific texts than on vocabulary lists
questions.explanation: Paragraph 2: on an early test, 'rereaders often perform as well as, or slightly better than, the recall group'.

questions.prompt: What can be inferred about learners who rely on rereading?
options: They may overestimate how much they will remember.
They usually forget material within a few minutes.
They find retrieval practice too easy to be useful.
They remember more after a delay than at first.
questions.explanation: Rereading creates 'a sense of familiarity that learners mistake for durable knowledge', so they think they know more than they will retain.

questions.prompt: Why does the author mention spacing practice sessions apart in paragraph 3?
options: To recommend a method that reduces the effort of studying
To describe a weakness in the experiments in paragraph 2
To contrast retrieval practice with a more effective technique
To show that the role of effort explains another finding
questions.explanation: Spacing is introduced with 'This helps explain why', as a further result accounted for by the idea that harder retrieval strengthens memory.

questions.prompt: Which of the following best expresses the main idea of the passage?
options: Tests are an unreliable way of measuring what students know.

Rereading is the best strategy for a test soon after studying.
Any learning task that feels difficult improves long-term memory.
questions.explanation: The passage argues that retrieving information 'is itself a powerful way of learning it', with the advantage appearing after a delay.

tasks.context: Listen to part of a talk in an astronomy class.

audio.speaker: Professor
audio.text: Okay, so last week a few of you asked why stars twinkle. It's a good question, and the answer actually has very little to do with the stars themselves. It's about our atmosphere. Astronomers call twinkling scintillation. Starlight travels through space in a straight line, but in the last tiny part of its journey it passes through layers of air with different temperatures. Warm air and cool air bend light slightly differently, and these layers are constantly moving. So the light gets pushed around, just a little, many times a second. Now, a star is so far away that it's basically a single point of light. When that one point gets pushed around, its brightness and position seem to flicker. Planets are different. Take Jupiter. It's much closer, so it appears as a tiny disc, not a point. Light from different parts of the disc is disturbed in different ways, and the flickers average out. That's why planets usually shine steadily. By the way, this is also why big modern telescopes are built on high mountains, above much of that moving air. Honestly, for astronomers, twinkling is mostly a nuisance. It's pretty, sure, but it blurs every image we take.

questions.explanation: Jupiter illustrates that a planet appears as a disc, so 'the flickers average out' and it shines steadily.

tasks.context: Listen to part of a talk in a linguistics class.

audio.speaker: Professor
audio.text: Today let's look at borrowing, which is when one language takes a word from another. English is a huge borrower. Think of 'piano' from Italian, 'yoghurt' from Turkish, or 'tsunami' from Japanese. But why do languages borrow? Usually for one of two reasons. The first is need. When speakers meet a new object or idea, they often just take the name that comes with it. English didn't have a word for that kind of wave, so 'tsunami' filled a gap. The second reason is prestige. Sometimes a language borrows words even when it already has perfectly good ones, because the other language is seen as fashionable or powerful. After the Norman Conquest, French was the language of the ruling class in England for centuries. That's why we have pairs like 'cow' and 'beef'. The animal kept its old English name, because the farmers who looked after it spoke English. But the meat on the table got a French name, because the people eating it spoke French. Now, borrowed words don't stay the same. They usually get adapted to the sounds and grammar of the new language, and after a few generations, most speakers simply don't notice they were ever foreign.

questions.prompt: What is the talk mainly about?
options: How English grammar changed after the Norman Conquest

How farmers in England named their animals
questions.explanation: The professor defines borrowing, gives two reasons for it and describes how borrowed words change.

questions.prompt: According to the professor, what is one reason languages borrow words?
options: To name things that are new to their speakers
To make their own grammar simpler
To replace words that are hard to pronounce
To help children learn to read
questions.explanation: The first reason is need: speakers meeting 'a new object or idea' take the name that comes with it.

questions.prompt: Why does the professor mention 'cow' and 'beef'?
options: To show that borrowed words change their sounds
To give an example of borrowing out of need
To explain why English farmers learned French
To illustrate borrowing based on prestige
questions.explanation: The pair follows her point that French was the powerful language of the ruling class, which is borrowing for prestige.

questions.prompt: What can be inferred about borrowed words in English?
options: Most of them are less than a hundred years old.

questions.explanation: She says that after a few generations 'most speakers simply don't notice they were ever foreign'.

tasks.context: Listen to part of a talk in a biology class.

audio.speaker: Professor
audio.text: Today I want to talk about how young songbirds learn to sing. Many people think birds are born knowing their songs. For some birds, that's true. But for songbirds like the zebra finch, singing is learned, a bit like a child learning to talk. In zebra finches, it's the males that sing, and learning happens in two stages. First, the young male listens. He hears an adult male, usually his father, and he remembers the song. At this stage, he doesn't sing much at all. Second, the young bird practises. His first attempts sound quiet and messy, so scientists sometimes call this stage babbling, just like a baby. Over many weeks, the bird compares his own singing with the song he remembers, and slowly the song gets better. Scientists have tested this. When a young zebra finch grows up without hearing any adult birds, he still sings, but his song sounds strange and incomplete. So listening early in life is very important. I think this is one of the clearest examples of learning in the animal world.

questions.prompt: What is the talk mainly about?
options: Why birds sing early in the morning

questions.prompt: What does the young bird do in the first stage?

He sings very loudly.
He copies other young birds.
He practises every morning.
questions.explanation: 'First, the young male listens' to an adult male and remembers the song.

questions.prompt: Why does the professor mention babies?
options: To show that birds learn faster than babies
To explain why parents sing to children
To compare early bird songs to early human speech
To describe a bird's first weeks of life
questions.explanation: The messy first songs are called babbling, 'just like a baby', comparing them to early speech.

questions.prompt: What can be inferred from the experiment the professor describes?

questions.explanation: Birds raised without hearing adults sing a 'strange and incomplete' song, so hearing adults is needed for a normal one.

tasks.context: Listen to part of a talk in an art history class.

audio.speaker: Professor
audio.text: Let's turn to something we tend to overlook in old paintings: the colours themselves, or rather, the pigments. Today you can pick a tube of blue paint off a shelf without a second thought. But for a Renaissance painter, blue was a serious business decision. The finest blue, ultramarine, was made by grinding up lapis lazuli, a stone mined mainly in what's now Afghanistan. It had to travel thousands of kilometres, and extracting the pigment was slow and wasteful. Weight for weight, ultramarine could cost more than gold. So what did that mean in practice? Well, contracts between painters and the people paying for the work sometimes specified exactly how much ultramarine had to be used, and where. It was saved for the most important figure in the picture, while cheaper blues, like azurite, went into skies and backgrounds. In other words, if you know what to look for, the pigment tells you what the patron valued most. Then, in the 1820s, a French chemist found a way to make ultramarine artificially, and the price collapsed. Painters could suddenly be generous with blue. I'd argue that's not a footnote: it quietly changed what painters felt free to do.

questions.prompt: What is the talk mainly about?
options: How Renaissance painters mixed their colours
Why skies in old paintings often look faded
How the cost of a pigment shaped its use in painting
Where lapis lazuli is mined and traded today
questions.explanation: The talk explains how ultramarine's high price decided where it was used, and what changed when it became cheap.

questions.prompt: According to the professor, what did some painting contracts state?
options: The date the painting had to be finished
How much ultramarine had to be used
Which colour the sky should be painted
Where the painter had to buy pigments
questions.explanation: Contracts 'specified exactly how much ultramarine had to be used, and where'.

questions.prompt: Why does the professor mention azurite?
options: To name the stone ultramarine was made from
To explain why ultramarine became cheaper
To show that blue was rarely used in skies
To contrast a less valued blue with ultramarine
questions.explanation: Azurite is a 'cheaper' blue used for skies and backgrounds, in contrast to ultramarine saved for the main figure.

questions.prompt: What is the professor's opinion of the invention of artificial ultramarine?
options: It had a significant effect on painting.
It is only a minor detail in art history.
It lowered the quality of later paintings.
It mattered more to chemists than to painters.
questions.explanation: He says 'that's not a footnote: it quietly changed what painters felt free to do'.

tasks.context: Listen to part of a talk in a sociology class.

audio.speaker: Professor
audio.text: So, here's a question. If you're looking for a job, who's most likely to help you find one: your close friends, or people you barely know? Most of you would say close friends. They care about you, after all. But in the 1970s, the sociologist Mark Granovetter interviewed people who'd recently changed jobs, and he found something counterintuitive. Many of them had heard about the job through acquaintances, people they saw only occasionally. He called these relationships weak ties.

audio.speaker: Student
audio.text: But wouldn't your close friends be more motivated to help?

audio.speaker: Professor
audio.text: They might be, yes. The catch is what they know. Your close friends tend to know each other, move in the same circles and hear the same news. So by the time something reaches you through them, you've probably heard it already. An acquaintance, on the other hand, is a bridge to a whole different network, with information you'd never come across otherwise. Now, I don't want to oversell this. Later studies suggest strong ties still matter a great deal, for emotional support, say, or when jobs are scarce. But the core insight has held up remarkably well: the people on the edges of your life may be the ones who open new doors.

questions.prompt: What is the main topic of the talk?
options: The value of distant acquaintances in finding opportunities
Why close friendships are difficult to maintain
How employers choose between job applicants
Methods sociologists use when interviewing people
questions.explanation: The talk presents Granovetter's finding that 'weak ties' often lead people to jobs and explains why.

questions.prompt: According to the professor, why are close friends less useful as a source of job information?
options: They are often too busy to help.
They prefer not to discuss work.
They usually hear the same news as you.
They tend to work in other cities.
questions.explanation: Close friends 'move in the same circles and hear the same news', so you've probably heard it already.

questions.prompt: Why does the professor describe an acquaintance as 'a bridge'?
options: To suggest that acquaintances are hard to reach
To show how acquaintances link people to new networks
To explain how Granovetter found his participants
To argue that friendships need constant effort
questions.explanation: The bridge image explains that an acquaintance connects you to 'a whole different network' with new information.

questions.prompt: What is the professor's attitude toward Granovetter's finding?
options: She thinks later research has disproved it.
She believes it applies only to the 1970s.
She considers it too obvious to be interesting.
She accepts it but warns against exaggerating it.
questions.explanation: She says 'I don't want to oversell this' yet adds that 'the core insight has held up remarkably well'.

items.prompt: What do you usually do on weekends?
items.explanation: Frequency adverbs go before the main verb: I always play football on Saturdays.

items.prompt: Excuse me, where is the campus bookstore?
items.explanation: 'Right' intensifies the preposition 'next to': It's right next to the cafeteria.

items.prompt: Is the pharmacy on Hill Street still open?
items.explanation: An indirect question uses statement order (subject before verb): Sorry, I don't know what time it closes.

items.prompt: How long have you lived in this city?
items.explanation: Present perfect with 'since' plus a past-tense clause: I have lived here since I started university.

items.prompt: Do you like your new laptop?
items.explanation: 'Much' modifies the comparatives, and 'than' introduces the thing compared: Yes, it's much lighter and faster than my old one.

items.prompt: Have you handed in your lab report yet?
items.explanation: Negative auxiliary + 'have to' + passive infinitive: Not yet. It doesn't have to be submitted until Friday.

items.prompt: What happened to the old sofa in the student lounge?
items.explanation: With a pronoun object, a phrasal verb is separated ('throw it away', not 'throw away it'): The staff decided to throw it away because it was broken.

items.prompt: Who is that woman talking to the dean?
items.explanation: 'Whose' + noun opens the relative clause, followed by subject and verb: She's the professor whose book we read last semester.

items.prompt: Have the research groups sent you their survey results?
items.explanation: 'Neither of' takes a singular verb and pronoun in formal English: No, neither of the groups has sent its results yet.

items.prompt: Why didn't you come to the review session this afternoon?
items.explanation: An inverted third conditional replaces 'if': Had I known the session was being held today, I would have come.
